mainEntity.name: Does fibromyalgia automatically rule out dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — fibromyalgia does not automatically mean dental implants are unsuitable. However, it does mean that a thorough individual assessment is essential before any treatment is planned. Factors such as bone density, medication use, associated oral health conditions, and general health status all need to be carefully evaluated. Many people with well-managed fibromyalgia may be considered suitable candidates after appropriate assessment. Your dentist will advise based on your specific clinical situation.

mainEntity.name: Can fibromyalgia medications affect dental implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some medications used to manage fibromyalgia — including certain antidepressants, anticonvulsants, and NSAIDs — may have implications for healing, bone metabolism, or bleeding. It is important to provide your dental team with a full and up-to-date medication list before any treatment is discussed. Your dentist may liaise with your GP or specialist to ensure that all relevant medical considerations are accounted for in your care plan.

mainEntity.name: Why do people with fibromyalgia often experience oral health problems?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fibromyalgia is associated with several oral health challenges. These may include dry mouth caused by medications, heightened sensitivity around the jaw and teeth, a greater prevalence of temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorder, bruxism (teeth grinding), and difficulties maintaining consistent oral hygiene routines on high-fatigue days. These factors do not make good oral health unattainable, but they do highlight the importance of regular dental monitoring and open communication with your dentist about your condition.

mainEntity.name: Is dental implant surgery painful for someone with fibromyalgia?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pain experience is highly individual, and for people with fibromyalgia, central sensitisation means pain signals may be amplified. Dental implant placement is performed under local anaesthesia, and sedation options may also be available for patients who are particularly anxious or sensitive. Post-operative discomfort is normal following any minor surgical procedure. Your dental team can work with you to develop an appropriate pain management plan. Discussing your pain sensitivity and any concerns before the procedure is strongly encouraged.

mainEntity.name: What should I tell my dentist about my fibromyalgia before a consultation?

acceptedAnswer.text: You should inform your dentist about your fibromyalgia diagnosis, how long you have had it, how well it is currently managed, and any medications you are taking — including doses and frequency. It is also helpful to mention any associated conditions you experience, such as TMJ issues, dry mouth, bruxism, or anxiety. Sharing relevant letters from your GP or rheumatologist can also assist your dental team in understanding your full medical picture.

mainEntity.name: Are there alternatives to dental implants for people with fibromyalgia?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — dental implants are one of several options for replacing missing teeth. Depending on your individual circumstances, a dentist may discuss alternatives such as a dental bridge or a removable partial or full denture. Each option has its own advantages and considerations. The best solution for you will depend on your oral health, bone structure, general health, and personal preferences. A comprehensive consultation will help you understand all available options and make an informed decision.
